irrelevant

ih-REL-uh-vunt — stress the REL; if it's irrelevant, it's not relevant — it just doesn't matter here. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Irrelevant is not connected to the matter at hand; having no bearing on the topic.

The lawyer objected that the question was irrelevant to the case.

Example

During a debate about the school lunch menu, a student stands up and describes his summer beach trip in loving detail — a story entirely irrelevant to the topic. The room goes quiet, and the moderator politely asks him to sit down.

His story has no bearing whatsoever on the lunch-menu question. Unlike 'wrong,' an irrelevant point can be perfectly true; it just doesn't apply to the topic.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unrelated: Unrelated states a plain fact about two things: they have no connection to each other at all — soccer and algebra, say. Irrelevant is a judgment made inside a discussion: this point, true or not, has no bearing on the matter being decided. Facts are unrelated; contributions are irrelevant.

immaterial: Immaterial means of no importance to the matter — a fact may be connected to the case, yet change nothing about its outcome. Irrelevant says the fact never bore on the topic in the first place. Lawyers call a connected-but-harmless detail immaterial and an off-topic one irrelevant.

beside the point: Beside the point describes a remark that answers something near the real issue but not the issue itself. Irrelevant is broader and blunter: the remark has no bearing on the topic at all. A comment can be beside the point while circling the subject; an irrelevant one never touches it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

relevant: directly related to the matter

pertinent: applying directly to the topic

Where it sits · how little it connects to anything

tangential → irrelevant → meaningless

tangential vs. irrelevant: Tangential is weaker than irrelevant — a tangential comment is at least loosely connected to the topic, while an irrelevant one has no connection at all.

meaningless vs. irrelevant: Meaningless is stronger than irrelevant: an irrelevant fact simply doesn't apply here, but a meaningless one carries no significance in any context.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ir-: not (the form Latin in- takes before r)

Prefix — re-: again, back (Latin)

Root — lev: to lift, to raise (from Latin levare, 'to lift')

Suffix — -ant: adjective-forming, 'doing' (Latin)

Put it together: Ir- ('not' — the form in- takes before r) + re- ('again, back') + lev ('to lift, to raise' — from Latin levare) + -ant (adjective-forming): Latin relevare meant 'to lift up' — a relevant point 'bears upon' the matter, carrying weight in the discussion. Add ir- and you get irrelevant: lifting nothing, carrying no weight on the topic.

Use the root in a new word: elevate: The crane elevated the steel beam to the top floor.

Word Building

Word Choice

Irrelevant is used to set aside points that don't bear on the topic, usually with 'to' — 'irrelevant to the case,' 'irrelevant to the argument.'
